case.case_title: Channa Pieris and Others v. Attorney-General and Others (Ratawesi Peramuna Case)
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Applications Nos. 146/92 to 154/92 and 155/92, decided on 17 February 1994

clause.text: General restrictions may apply for national security, public order, health, morality, and welfare.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the arrests and detentions of the petitioners under the Emergency Regulations were lawful and in accordance with the procedure established by law, and whether the restrictions on fundamental rights under the Constitution were justified under Article 15(7).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that their fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2), 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(c) were violated by unlawful arrest and detention without proper procedure and without being informed of the reasons for arrest, and that the Emergency Regulations did not justify such restrictions.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioners were lawfully arrested and detained under the Emergency Regulations made under the Public Security Ordinance, and that the restrictions on fundamental rights were valid under Article 15(7) of the Constitution in the interests of national security and public order.
key_facts: Petitioners were members of the Ratawesi Peramuna, an anti-government movement.
They were arrested on 27 February 1992 at a meeting at Kawduduwa temple based on police suspicion of conspiracy to overthrow the government.
Arrests were made without warrants under Emergency Regulations, specifically Regulation 18(1).
Detention orders were issued under Regulations 17 and 19, but with procedural irregularities and questionable authority.
The petitioners were not informed of the true reasons for their arrest at the time.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that while Article 15(7) permits restrictions on fundamental rights in the interests of national security and public order, such restrictions must be prescribed by law and comply with procedural safeguards. The Emergency Regulations must be properly invoked and followed. Arrests and detentions must be in accordance with procedure established by law, and persons arrested must be informed of the reasons for arrest. Vague suspicions and procedural irregularities do not satisfy these requirements.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the arrests were not made in accordance with the procedure established by law under the Emergency Regulations. The police failed to establish reasonable grounds for suspicion of an offence under the Regulations. Detention orders were issued without proper authority and were ultra vires. The petitioners were not informed of the reasons for arrest at the time, violating Article 13(1). The Court emphasized that mere membership in a lawful organization or harsh political criticism does not justify arrest under the Emergency Regulations. The restrictions under Article 15(7) do not permit arbitrary or unlawful deprivation of liberty.
principles_established: Restrictions on fundamental rights under Article 15(7) must be prescribed by law and comply with procedural safeguards.
Arrest and detention must be in accordance with procedure established by law, including reasonable grounds for suspicion.
Persons arrested must be informed promptly of the reasons for arrest to enable them to challenge it.
Vague suspicions or hopes of finding evidence do not justify arrest or detention.
Police and authorities must not act arbitrarily or ultra vires when invoking Emergency Regulations.

outcome.holding: The Court declared that the fundamental rights of the petitioners under Article 13(1) of the Constitution were violated because the arrests and detentions were not made in accordance with procedure established by law, and the petitioners were not informed of the reasons for their arrest. The restrictions under Article 15(7) did not justify the violations. The Court ordered solatium payments to the petitioners for the violations.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Each petitioner except one was ordered to be paid Rs. 5,000 as solatium; the petitioner not present at the meeting was ordered Rs. 10,000.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 15(7) was central to the respondents' defense that the Emergency Regulations justified the arrests and detentions. The Court analyzed whether the restrictions imposed were lawful under Article 15(7) and found that the procedural requirements were not met, thus the restrictions were not valid under this clause.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found that the arrests were not made in accordance with the procedure established by law under the Emergency Regulations, that the petitioners were not reasonably suspected of offences under the Regulations, and that the detention orders were ultra vires. The petitioners were not informed of the reasons for arrest, violating Article 13(1).
